\begin{abstract}
We investigate how reliably text can be sent using binary light signalling.
A patch on a Mac screen displays white for one and black for zero; a phone
records a video of these changes. Software reads the brightness to recover
the bits and reconstruct the text. We disturb reception by shining light
onto the screen or blocking the camera's view.
Across 21 videos, we test three ways of adding extra bits to help repair
errors: repetition, Hamming and Reed--Solomon coding. We measure message
recovery and transmission time. We also test whether measuring brightness
differently or rearranging bits before transmission improves recovery.
The receiver restores the original bit order before decoding. Brightness
methods process the same videos, so each faces the same recorded interference.
Measuring a larger screen area raises observed recovery from 8/12 to 12/12
messages in the main glare tests. Interleaved Hamming has higher observed
recovery than its non-interleaved counterpart, whereas interleaved
Reed--Solomon has lower recovery in the recorded blockage trials.
Because these transmissions experienced different disturbances, controlled
simulations complement the physical results by examining how error
grouping affects correction. These findings show
that adding protection alone is insufficient: its effectiveness depends
on the errors encountered. Small samples and manually varied disturbances
limit wider conclusions.
\end{abstract}
\begin{IEEEkeywords}
optical communication, error correction, interleaving, sampling, experimental design
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
We investigate reliable text transmission using binary light signalling.
A Mac screen shows each message as white and black flashes representing
ones and zeros. A phone records these changes as a video, which software reads
to reconstruct the text. This screen--camera approach,
also explored in PixNet~\cite{pixnet}, allows us to observe how glare and
blockage disturb reception.

These disturbances can change the brightness readings, causing errors in
the recovered text. Error-correcting codes add extra bits to repair some
mistakes, but take longer to transmit. We therefore examine which errors
occur, whether the codes address them, and what further improvements are
needed.

We first explain the communication system (Section~\ref{sec:system}) and
experimental design (Section~\ref{sec:design}), then compare the codes
through their message recovery and transmission time (Section~\ref{sec:physical}).
The observed failures motivate two extensions: improving how brightness is
measured (Section~\ref{sec:receiver}), and rearranging bits during transmission
to spread consecutive errors before correction (Section~\ref{sec:interleaving}).
We evaluate brightness methods on the same
videos and use controlled computer simulations to complement physical
trials of coding and bit order. We conclude by
assessing the findings and limitations of the evidence (Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}).

\section{Building and Understanding the Link}
\label{sec:system}
\subsection{Sending Text as Light}
The transmitter converts text into UTF-8 bytes, each containing eight bits.
A Python program displays these bits as white or black, holding each for
200 ms. The phone records the screen at approximately 30 frames/s, giving
about six images per bit. Recorded timestamps locate measurements despite
uneven frame spacing.

To distinguish messages, we organise each transmission into a \emph{packet}:
\begin{center}\footnotesize
8 guard bits $\to$ 32-bit preamble $\to$ 48-bit header\\
$\to$ coded message and CRC $\to$ 8 guard bits.
\end{center}
The \emph{preamble} is a known pattern for locating the message and
measuring dark and bright levels. The header identifies the code, length, version
and sequence; dark guards separate packets. Header and message each carry
a 16-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC), calculated from their contents to
detect changes. Only the message and its CRC receive error correction.
When bits are rearranged, both ends use the same predefined order;
the header does not record it.

We use 1920$\times$1080 iPhone 15 and 15 Pro videos.

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=.9\columnwidth]{campaign_setup.pdf}
\caption{Top: recorded screen with central ROI (blue), larger patch
and tiles (orange), and references (pink, each split in two).
Bottom: illustrative four-pixel average; actual regions contain many pixels.
Both central and larger-patch means give one brightness value per frame.}
\label{fig:setup}\end{figure}

\subsection{Reading Bits from Video}
We average grayscale pixels inside the blue region in Fig.~\ref{fig:setup},
turning each image into a brightness measurement. Its width and height are
about 20\% of the visible patch, chosen from unobstructed frames without
testing which region decodes best. The receiver finds the preamble and
uses the midpoint between its dark and bright levels as a threshold.
For each bit, it takes the median brightness within the middle half of the
200 ms interval, avoiding many display transitions. Values above the
threshold become ones; the rest become zeros.

The receiver estimates packet start from the known preamble but fixes
bit duration at the transmitter's configured 200 ms. Estimating duration
from the preamble caused later sampling intervals to drift out of
alignment in pilot trials. The fixed-duration approach recovered 16/16
pilot messages without errors in 3,840 body bits. This development result
guided main analysis; it is not independent validation. The header must
pass its CRC before the message is decoded and checked. Expected message
text is never supplied to the receiver or used to select timing.

\subsection{Correcting Errors and Paying for Redundancy}
Without coding, each message bit is sent once. \textbf{Repetition} sends
three or five copies and takes their majority: \texttt{000} received as
\texttt{010} still gives zero, but \texttt{110} does not. Three copies
tolerate one error per group; five tolerate two.

\textbf{Hamming$(7,4)$} adds three parity bits to four data bits. Each
parity check requires an even number of ones in an overlapping set of
positions~\cite{hamming}. Together, the failed checks give a \emph{syndrome}
that locates one wrong bit (Fig.~\ref{fig:hamming}). Flipping it repairs
that word; two errors can instead identify the wrong position.

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{campaign_hamming.pdf}
\caption{Verified Hamming example. Circles show which positions each parity
check covers; position 5 belongs to checks 1 and 4.}
\label{fig:hamming}\end{figure}

\textbf{Reed--Solomon} instead protects bytes. The credited
\texttt{reedsolo} library adds four parity bytes and corrects up to
two damaged bytes~\cite{reedsolomon,reedsolo}. Several wrong bits within
one byte count as one damaged byte; one wrong bit in each of three
bytes exceeds the limit. After correction, CRC detects many remaining
errors but neither repairs them nor guarantees the original message.
Including CRC and framing, an eight-byte message takes 99.2 s with five-copy
repetition versus 47.2 s with Hamming. Better recovery must therefore justify
the added transmission time.

\section{Experimental Design and Evidence}
\label{sec:design}
\subsection{Stages, Controls and Measurement Units}
Table~\ref{tab:questions} separates development, code evaluation and
acquisition stress across 21 videos. Payloads are four, eight and twelve
bytes: \texttt{A7k2}, \texttt{A7k2M9q4}, and \texttt{A7k2M9q4R6v8}.
They standardise content within each length and include mixed character
patterns. Because each length has only one message and the strings share
a prefix, length and content effects cannot be separated.

Main blockage testing uses seven configurations: uncoded, repetition
$\times3$, repetition $\times5$, Hamming and Reed--Solomon without
interleaving (depth one), plus Hamming and Reed--Solomon at depth eight.
Each occurs at three lengths in two rounds, giving six packets per
configuration. The ordinary Hamming/Reed--Solomon controls are reused for
the interleaving comparison; they are not counted twice. Body-glare testing
compares uncoded and Hamming at each length and round. Acquisition-stress
tests instead apply early glare to uncoded, Hamming and Reed--Solomon
transmissions of the long message.

\subsection{Experimental Controls}
Transmitter logs verify each packet's message, code, interleaving depth,
order and timing. Receiver settings remain fixed during main analysis,
and all seven processing methods use the same 42 blockage and 12 glare
packets. Each method therefore encounters identical recorded interference.

Physical interventions target 1.2 s, but manual duration, coverage and
intensity vary. Comparisons between separately disturbed coded packets
therefore describe performance under the recorded conditions; receiver
comparisons on the same videos provide stronger control. Failures and
packets with no observed errors remain in the analysis.

\subsection{Outcomes and Statistical Scope}
Success requires both exact payload agreement and a valid CRC. Failures
are retained by stage: acquisition/header, sampling, error correction or
payload CRC. Body bit-error rate (BER) is the fraction of received body
bits that differ from those sent, before correction. Missing bodies are
unavailable, not zero BER.

To account for the cost of redundancy, we also measure goodput: correctly
delivered payload bits per second of transmission. For $n_i$ coded-body
bits and $b_i$ payload bits, packet duration $T_i$ and overall goodput $G$ are
\begin{equation}
T_i=0.2(96+n_i),\qquad
G=\frac{\sum_i b_i\,\mathbf{1}(\text{exact+CRC})}{\sum_i T_i}.
\end{equation}
The indicator is one only for exact recovery with a valid CRC. Every included packet contributes its transmission duration to the denominator, including packets that fail. Transmission time includes
96 framing intervals but excludes the 0.2 s lead-in, eight-second gaps,
setup and offline processing.

Physical results show counts and individual outcomes: bits within a
packet and packets sharing a video are not independent observations.
Two rounds provide limited repetition, so we avoid significance tests or
narrow intervals for physical code rankings. Simulation intervals instead
quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty under the specified noise model.

\section{Physical Results: Errors and Coding}
\label{sec:physical}
\subsection{Observed Errors and Detection Failures}
The clean pilot recovers 16/16 messages without errors in 3,840 body bits.
Under the main disturbances, the receiver detects all 54 packets but
recovers only 35 messages: the failures occur after detection. Clean
reception establishes that the link can work.

Glare produces 18/1,320 wrong bits (1.36\%), all $0\!\to\!1$:
dark symbols are read as bright. Blockage produces 78/7,344 (1.06\%),
with 34 $0\!\to\!1$ and 44 $1\!\to\!0$ errors. Rejecting unusually
bright readings may therefore address glare, but cannot address both
directions of blockage error.

Runs of at least two consecutive wrong bits account for 44/78 blockage
errors (56\%) and 14/18 glare errors (78\%) in Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}.
Most errors therefore occur in clusters, particularly under glare.
Several errors within one protected group can exceed its correction limit
even when overall BER is low. This motivates interleaving, which changes
how consecutive errors reach those groups.

\begin{figure}[t]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{campaign_noise.pdf}
\caption{Top: example glare recording and wrong-bit centres.
Bottom: 51 blockage and ten glare error runs across 54 main packets;
packet boundaries terminate runs. Runs do not measure disturbance duration:
a disturbed bit may remain correct. Zero-error packets remain in delivery results.}
\label{fig:noise}\end{figure}

Body-glare recovery is 8/12, with all four failures in one capture setup
and no baseline body errors in the other eight packets. This limits claims
of consistent glare robustness. Early glare instead prevents all six
packets from yielding valid headers; body BER is unavailable. Here,
recovery requires protecting the starting pattern or header before body
correction can help.

\subsection{Message Recovery and Transmission Cost}
Table~\ref{tab:physical} compares the seven blockage configurations, with
individual outcomes in Fig.~\ref{fig:packets}. Repetition $\times5$
recovers 5/6 messages versus 3/6 for $\times3$, but goodput rises only
from 0.476 to 0.538 bit/s because the extra copies take longer to send.
Reed--Solomon without interleaving recovers 6/6 and achieves the highest
observed goodput, 1.538 bit/s. Recorded recovery is higher for interleaved
Hamming and lower for interleaved Reed--Solomon than for their respective
non-interleaved configurations. These separately disturbed transmissions
do not isolate the effect of interleaving;
Section~\ref{sec:interleaving} investigates this contrast.

Repetition $\times5$ has lower BER than non-interleaved Reed--Solomon
(0.42\% versus 1.79\%), yet lower recovery and goodput. Extra copies
can dilute one disturbance's errors across more transmitted bits.
Lower BER alone therefore does not establish better communication;
message recovery and transmission cost must also be considered.

Recovery falls from 35/54 to 30/54 when using the earliest available
completed recordings.
This sensitivity to recording selection limits claims about reliability
in new conditions.

\section{Extension 1: Receiver Processing}
\label{sec:receiver}
\subsection{Receiver Comparisons}
We compare seven methods on the same frames. The screen displays one bit
across the whole transmitting patch, but local glare can dominate a small
central region of interest (ROI). A larger-patch mean averages brightness
over a wider area, allowing unaffected pixels to dilute that glare
(Fig.~\ref{fig:setup}). It cannot remove glare covering the entire region.
We use the inner 80\% of the patch's width and height, or a fourfold
enlargement of the central box where full bounds are unavailable.

Reference compensation addresses lighting changes shared across the image.
Because the reference strips do not carry the changing message, their
brightness changes can estimate this disturbance. We subtract the median
change across four reference regions, relative to their preamble levels,
from the larger-patch mean. This relies on similar illumination changes
at the references and signal; obstructed references can mislead it.

Spatial processing addresses glare concentrated in part of the patch.
We divide the region into $4\times4$ tiles, normalise each using its
preamble dark and bright levels, and take the lower quartile of valid
readings. This favours darker tiles that glare may have spared, rather
than letting bright tiles pull up the average. At least half the tiles
must have 20 grayscale units of contrast. Dark blockage can bias this
choice; the combined method applies reference compensation before spatial
processing.

Temporal filtering smooths the larger-patch mean, using the expectation
that brightness remains steady within each bit. The exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) blends
successive measurements; Kalman filtering weights the previous estimate
and new measurement using estimated uncertainty~\cite{kalman}. Smoothing
may suppress brief fluctuations, but must preserve genuine bit transitions.
Both use actual frame intervals $\Delta t_i$: EWMA uses
$a_i=1-\exp(-\Delta t_i/0.025)$; Kalman process variance is
$160000\Delta t_i$, with measurement and initial variance 400.
Their new-measurement weights at 30 frames/s are approximately 0.74 and
0.93, favouring responsiveness over strong smoothing. Neither can recover
a signal completely hidden by sustained blockage.

Settings were fixed using development data. All methods share baseline
packet detection and timing, then calibrate their brightness thresholds
from the known preamble. Expected message text is never supplied to the
decoder, so the comparison tests measurement changes after detection.

\section{Extension 2: Interleaving and Controlled Noise}
\label{sec:interleaving}
\subsection{Reordering Bits Before Correction}
Suppose a short blockage causes three consecutive bit errors. If all
three fall in one Hamming word, they exceed its one-error correction limit.
In a simple three-word example, interleaving sends one bit from word A,
then B, then C, repeating this order. After the receiver restores the
original order, each word has one error and all three can be repaired.
Interleaving has not removed errors; it has distributed them into groups
the code can correct.

Our implementation writes coded bits across eight rows and transmits them
down columns, skipping empty positions. The receiver reverses this order
before correction. No bits or transmission airtime are added; buffering
latency is unmeasured. Reed--Solomon illustrates why this is not always
helpful: it corrects two damaged bytes across the body. Several wrong bits
within one byte still count as one damaged byte, but spreading them into
three bytes exceeds its correction limit.

Physical Hamming recovery rises from 4/6 to 6/6 with interleaving, although
raw errors rise from nine to eleven. Reed--Solomon falls from 6/6 to 2/6:
its four interleaved failures damage 3, 7, 3 and 4 bytes. All non-interleaved
packets damage at most two bytes, including one with four wrong bits.
Table~\ref{tab:mapping} shows two recorded examples: separate Hamming
words each remain correctable, whereas four damaged Reed--Solomon bytes
exceed the budget.

All indices start at zero; packets experienced separate disturbances.}

\subsection{Controlled Noise Models}
Physical disturbances vary between transmissions. To compare coding and
bit order under shared noise, we use 480,000 simulated trials: 240 conditions
with 2,000 trials each. Comparisons share nine-byte payloads and noise sequences; longer coded
bodies encounter more of each sequence. Saved seeds reproduce the trials;
720 decodes were replayed during verification.

Independent noise flips each bit with probability $p$. To represent
clusters, a two-state model alternates between good and bad periods~\cite{gilbert}.
The long-run fraction of bad slots is $\rho$, and their mean consecutive
length is $L$ bit intervals. Its transition probabilities are
\begin{equation}
P(B\to G)=1/L,\qquad P(G\to B)=\rho/[(1-\rho)L].
\end{equation}
Good slots leave bits unchanged. Bad slots either flip bits or force them
to one, representing the direction observed under glare. Forced-one noise
leaves transmitted ones correct, so $\rho$ is not its BER. Initial states
use the stationary probabilities. We sweep $p$ or $\rho$ through
$0,0.01,0.025,0.05,0.10,0.20$, with $L=8$ for bursts, then test
$L=2,4,8,16$ at $\rho=0.05$. Only the coded body is disturbed;
packet detection and headers are ideal, but framing airtime is included.
These models test error mechanisms rather than reproduce a particular camera.

\subsection{Simulation Results and Design Implications}
Figure~\ref{fig:simulation} shows that interleaving's benefit depends on
both code and burst structure. Under correlated flips at $\rho=0.05$,
Hamming gains 39.0 percentage points at $L=4$ (95\% paired interval:
36.9--41.2), but 11.7 at $L=16$ (10.4--13.2). Reed--Solomon loses
30.75 and 13.85 points, respectively, and is harmed throughout the tested
length range under both burst models. The practical choice is therefore
the code and bit order together: spreading errors helps Hamming when it
keeps each word correctable, but can harm Reed--Solomon by damaging more
bytes. The smaller Hamming gain at $L=16$ also shows that the same
interleaver does not provide equal protection across burst lengths.

At fixed $\rho$, longer bad periods also occur less frequently, allowing
some short packets to avoid them entirely. The length sweep therefore
changes both the severity of an encounter and its likelihood. The plotted
intervals resample matched trial pairs and quantify uncertainty within
each model condition; more simulated trials do not provide more physical
recording conditions.

At $\rho=0.05$ and $L=8$, interleaved repetition $\times5$ recovers
72.90\% of messages under correlated flips, exceeding Hamming's 66.70\%.
Yet its goodput is only 0.490 bit/s versus 0.960 bit/s: the extra copies
improve delivery probability while nearly halving useful delivery rate.
Code selection therefore depends on whether reliable individual delivery
or useful throughput matters more. One simulated wrong payload passes
CRC; it remains a failure because success requires actual message recovery.

\section{Validation, Limitations and Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}
\subsection{Verification and Experimental Limits}
Saved logs, brightness traces and simulation seeds make the outcomes
reproducible. Tests check coding, correction limits, interleaving reversal,
and detection and sampling failures. Clean synthetic tests cover every
code, depth and receiver combination without supplying expected messages
to the decoder.
\input{report_figures/campaign_test_count.tex}

The receiver comparisons provide the clearest physical evidence because
each method processes identical recorded interference. Separate code
transmissions experience manually varied disturbances, while two rounds
and different capture setups limit conclusions about general reliability.
Section~\ref{sec:physical} also quantifies sensitivity to recording selection.
A follow-up should automate blockage and glare, test every condition across
setups, and use several messages per length. This would separate coding
effects from exposure and message content. Improving packet detection is
also necessary: the six early-glare failures occur before body correction
can help.

\balance
\subsection{Connection to the Module and Wider Practice}
Week 1's sampling ideas underpin the camera timing, brightness regions
and within-bit median. Measuring a wider region can help when repeated
samples of an obstructed region cannot. Week 2's repetition and Hamming
codes expose the redundancy--rate trade-off; Reed--Solomon and interleaving
extend it to different correction groups.

Weeks 2--3 connect uncertainty to its probability model. Our directional,
clustered errors violate the independent, symmetric assumptions of the
binary symmetric channel, so average BER alone cannot justify its capacity
formula. Lab 2's transmitter--channel--receiver experiment is implemented
optically. For robotics, this illustrates why sensor processing should
follow an understanding of how measurements fail.

\subsection{Conclusion}
We built a screen-to-camera link that transmits text through binary light
signals, then used physical recordings and controlled simulations to
investigate how glare and blockage affect recovery. The experiments showed
that reliable communication depends on where errors arise and how they
are grouped, as well as how many occur.

Measuring a larger screen area raised glare recovery from 8/12 to 12/12
without additional filtering. Interleaving helped Hamming by distributing
errors across independently correctable words, but harmed the tested
Reed--Solomon configuration by spreading damage across too many bytes.
These findings show why a more elaborate receiver or additional protection
is not automatically better: each change must address the observed failure
mechanism and justify its transmission cost.

The clearest next step is to strengthen packet detection, since all six
transmissions with glare over the starting pattern failed before body
correction could help. Repeated starting patterns and error-protected
headers are concrete options to test. Automated disturbances would then
allow these changes and coding choices to be compared under repeatable
interference. The resulting design should preserve the benefits of broader
brightness measurement while selecting coding and bit order together,
judging success through both recovered messages and useful bits delivered
per second.
